newsitem.title: RWANDA: Zaire spurns talks despite Tutsi offensive.
newsitem.headline: Zaire spurns talks despite Tutsi offensive.

text.p: Zaire defiantly rejected peace talks with its neighbours despite fears that victories by advancing ethnic Tutsi rebels could herald the disintegration of the vast Central African nation.
The conflict in eastern Zaire assumed greater international dimensions with the government adding Uganda to the list of its enemies and more world leaders urging round table peace negotiations.

"The government will not undertake any negotiation, will not participate in any regional conference while a part of national territory is occupied by foreign forces," Prime Minister Kengo wa Dondo told an emergency session of parliament.

"This war which the combined forces of Uganda, Burundi and Rwanda are waging against Zaire has brought to broad daylight Rwanda's intention not to welcome on its territory its nationals living in Zaire and to pursue its insane plan of annexing a part of our territory."

Kenyan state radio said Kenya planned to host a summit of seven African countries on November 5 but did not say if the main subject would be the war in eastern Zaire, where Banyamulenge Tutsi rebels have seized a string of towns.

France, the United Nations and the Organisation of African Unity (OAU) called for talks to resolve a conflict which threatened the lives of more than half a million refugees who fled to Zaire to escape ethnic strife in Rwanda and Burundi.

Fighting raged near Goma, the most important town in the region, on Thursday and aid agencies which had been responsible for feeding the Hutu refugees prepared to evacuate the area, aid officials said.
The rebel victories raised a serious prospect that Zaire could collapse as a nation while ailing President Mobutu Sese Seseko, in power for more than 30 years, lay sick in Europe.

The Zaire government's hardening tone appeared only matched by fears of Western intervention, notably by France which sent paratroops to Rwanda in 1994 on what Paris called a humanitarian mission to help millions of refugees.
Tutsis who had seized power in Rwanda accused France then of intervening to protect its Hutu allies who lost a civil war after ethnic slaughter in which up to a million Tutsis were massacred.
"If foreigners come to help Mobutu and his political clique you should help us to fight them," rebel commander Laurent Kabila told reporters in Uvira, one of the towns captured by the Tutis.
The Banyamulenge Tutsis, whose ancestors settled from Rwanda 200 years ago, say they are fighting Zaire's attempts to expel them.
Zaire accuses Rwanda and Burundi, both ruled by Tutsis, of backing its rebel foes. It says Rwanda has designs on Zairean territory to make room for pan-Tutsi empire.
Rwanda has openly admitted that units of its Tutsi-dominated army did enter Zaire and some independent sources also see the hand of Burundi's Tutsi army in the fighting.

Zaire's Defence Minister Admiral Mavua Mudima denied reports that part of Goma had fallen into enemy hands. "We have temporarily lost control of the Rusizi plain in South Kivu and of Kibumba in North Kivu, but Goma is still in our hands," he told parliament.
Mavua said Uganda, Rwanda and Burundi aimed to take over a 1,000 km (600-mile) strip of Zairean territory and had prepared 15 battalions to accomplish the goal.
